svg.title: The real dates behind Away in a Manger: 1868, eight unsigned lines appear in an American church newspaper; 1882, the carol resurfaces, still unsigned; 1883-84, around Luther's 400th birth anniversary, magazines start crediting it to Luther with no evidence; 1885, the first hymnal printing leaves the Luther claim out; 1887, James R. Murray's songbook repeats the Luther claim with the tune that became standard; 1892, an unsigned third verse completes the carol as sung today.
svg.desc: A vertical timeline of six dated entries. 1868: eight lines of the carol appear, unsigned, inside a Christmas story in the Protestant Churchman, an American church newspaper. 1882: the carol resurfaces, still with no author named, in The Congregationalist. 1883 to 1884: around Luther's 400th birth anniversary, magazines start crediting the carol to Luther and to the mothers of Germany, with no evidence supporting it. 1885: the first hymnal to print it, a Philadelphia songbook, leaves the Luther claim out. 1887: James R. Murray publishes it with a new tune in his own songbook and repeats the Luther claim; his tune is the one that caught on. 1892: a third verse, Be near me Lord Jesus, is added without a name in another songbook, completing the carol as it is sung today.
svg.text: The real dates behind “Away in a Manger”
Eight lines of the carol appear, unsigned, inside a Christmas story
in an American church newspaper, the Protestant Churchman.
The carol resurfaces, still with no author named,
in another American religious newspaper, The Congregationalist.
Around Luther's 400th birth anniversary, magazines start crediting
the carol to Luther and “the mothers of Germany.” No evidence supports it.
The first hymnal to print it, a Philadelphia songbook, leaves the
Luther claim out — its editors were careful not to repeat it.
James R. Murray publishes it with a new tune in his own songbook,
and repeats the Luther claim. His tune is the one that caught on.
A third verse, “Be near me, Lord Jesus,” is added without a name
in another songbook, completing the carol as it is sung today.
